2. The authors also mention “large experimental variability” in reporting battery testing metrics
such as cycle life, which is certainly true and is also apparent from Figures 3 and 5. So, I
commend the authors for reporting such true and large variations in the manuscript, which is
seldom reported in the literature. But my question is how to predict such large measurement
noise, i.e., aleatoric uncertainties? A Bayesian technique such as DKL can be used to predict
such aleatoric uncertainties, so the authors should check if their DKL model can indeed
reproduce the noise in their measurements. It will be highly beneficial to the community.
Our response: We thank the reviewer for this insightful comment and for highlighting the
importance of reporting large experimental variability. We agree that this aleatoric uncertainty
is an inherent and critical aspect of battery research that warrants more attention.
The central design principle of our work is to accelerate materials discovery via Bayesian
framework. Consequently, its primary function is to efficiently guide the search for high-
performing electrolyte formulations rather than to explicitly model or reproduce the statistical
distribution of the experimental noise.
Nevertheless, aleatoric uncertainty is implicitly managed within our Gaussian process with
deep kernel learning (GP-DKL) approach. The GP-DKL surrogate models the predictive
posterior distribution over the design space, and its variance term inherently captures the
uncertainty associated with its predictions. Our Thompson sampling-based acquisition function
leverages this full posterior distribution—not just the mean prediction—to balance exploration
and exploitation. By sampling from the surrogate, the algorithm naturally accounts for regions
of high uncertainty, which are influenced by both a lack of data (epistemic uncertainty) and
inherent measurement noise (aleatoric uncertainty). This optimization-focused approach is
particularly well-suited to our application context, where experimental evaluation of electrolyte
performance presents significant challenges: each sample requires ~3 months of testing time
and is subject to considerable experimental variability.
We agree with the reviewer that a direct assessment of the DKL model’s capability to
reproduce the observed aleatoric uncertainty would be a valuable contribution and an
interesting direction for future research. However, for the specific objective of this work—
accelerated optimization under severe experimental constraints—the key performance metric
is the efficiency of discovering optimal candidates. Therefore, the success of our framework is
best measured by its demonstrated ability to rapidly identify promising electrolyte formulations
with minimal experimental overhead, as shown through our active learning iterations and the
10
successful knowledge transfer.
2. The authors did not open source their codes, which is one of the requirements of the journal.
While they did provide access to their partial codebase, I would also need access to data,
model checkpoints and remaining codes in order to ensure it is fully reproducible. The provided
codebase is also not well-documented. So, I recommend that the authors upload all their codes,
datasets, and model checkpoints on GitHub and/or Zenodo with detailed documentation on how
to use it including the python libraries involved.
Our response: Thank you for your comment. All the codes and datasets have been uploaded to
GitHub (https://github.com/XWang1999/Electrolyte_Optimization_Deep_Active_Learning)
with detailed documentation specifying the Python library dependencies and step-by-step
instructions for reproducing the optimization workflow.
⚫ Our framework is designed as an online optimization process that operates in tandem with
sequential experimental measurements, where each experimental iteration informs the next
candidate selection. Accordingly, the released repository includes a demonstration
notebook (Electrolyte_Optimization_Demo_DAL.ipynb) that reproduces the full
optimization workflow using three active learning iterations, providing a transparent and
executable example of how the method operates in practice.
⚫ The Deep Kernel Learning (DKL) implementation is provided in the dknet folder, which
details the construction and training of the hybrid neural network–Gaussian process
surrogate. In addition, a numerical example implemented in DAL_numerical_demo.py
illustrates the optimization process on a benchmark test function, offering a clear
demonstration of how the DKL-based surrogate performs iterative learning and guides the
search toward optimal regions.
⚫ For optimization in expanded parameter spaces, the framework can be directly extended
by modifying the Target Statistic Coding (TSC) module according to the annotations and
explanations provided in the notebook. This procedure enables knowledge transfer
between tasks and has been explicitly described in both the manuscript and the released
code, ensuring that the workflow can be readily adapted for broader electrolyte design and
related optimization scenarios.
3. Why choose Thompson sampling as acquisition function over standard and more common
acquisition functions such as the expected improvement? There is no justification provided in
the draft.
Our response: We selected Thompson Sampling (TS) over standard acquisition functions like
Expected Improvement (EI) primarily for its superior and more straightforward scalability for
11
batch-parallel Bayesian Optimization [R1]. This is a critical requirement by our experimental
hardware.
Our experimental platform is a 32-channel battery cycler, which allows us to test 32 distinct
electrolyte formulations simultaneously. To fully leverage this capability and accelerate the
optimization process, we need select a diverse and promising batch of candidates at each
iteration, rather than a single point.
Thompson Sampling is well-suited for this batch scenario. To generate a batch of 𝑘
candidates (in our case, 𝑘=32), we can simply draw 𝑘 independent function samples from the
posterior of the Gaussian Process surrogate model. The location of the maximum of each
sample is then chosen as a candidate for the batch. This procedure is computationally efficient
and naturally promotes exploration and diversity within the batch, as each sample represents a different
plausible hypothesis of the true objective function.
In contrast, extending acquisition functions like EI to the batch setting is more complex. A naive
approach of simply selecting the top 𝑘 points with the highest EI values would result in a
highly redundant batch, with points clustered around a single peak in the acquisition function.
More sophisticated methods like q-Expected Improvement (q-EI) are required to properly
account for the joint improvement over a batch, but they come at a much higher computational
cost and implementation complexity [R2].
Given our experimental constraint of performing 32 parallel evaluations, Thompson Sampling
provides an elegant, scalable, and effective solution for maximizing the efficiency of our
discovery workflow.
To improve the justification, the text below has been inserted into the “Deep active
learning approach” Section of the revised manuscript: “To fully leverage the experimental
throughput of parallel evaluations, an acquisition function of Thompson Sampling (see
Methods) is then constructed based on the posterior distribution from the surrogate model of
DKL. This strategy enables scalable batch-parallel optimization and efficiently sample the
parameter space of electrolyte formulas by balancing exploration (i.e., testing regions with high
uncertainty) and exploitation (i.e., testing promising regions based on completed experiment
results) 50”
[R1] Kandasamy, K. et al. Parallelised Bayesian optimisation via Thompson sampling.
International Conference on Artificial Intelligence and Statistics. 133-142 (2018).
[R2] Gelbart, M.A. Constrained Bayesian Optimization and Applications. Harvard University,
2015.

4. a) The optimization is carried over only 13 molecular components (6 solvents, 4 salts, 3
additives) and later two more molecular components were added in the search space. While we
know that molecular chemical space is enormous, estimated to be on the order of 1060. So, is
their approach truly carrying out optimization over discrete electrolyte space then?
Our response: Thank you for this important question, which touches on a crucial distinction.
The reviewer is correct that the universal molecular chemical space is astronomically large. Our
work, however, is not designed to address that molecular generative space. Instead, it targets
the formulation compositional space, which is a practical and important challenge in
experimental battery research.
This compositional space arises from the combinatorial mixing of a pre-selected set of
viable components (solvents, salts, and additives). The primary bottleneck here is not
computational but experimental. Each data point—representing a single electrolyte
formulation—requires complex cell assembly, pre-conditioning, and months-long cycling tests
to evaluate performance. Furthermore, these battery-level evaluations suffer from significant
experimental noise, where identical formulations can yield considerable variations in cycle life.
Because of this extreme cost and inherent variability, typical experimental studies report only
a handful of formulations.
While our initial set of 13 components is modest, it generates a combinatorial space of
over 5,400 unique formulations—a number far too large to screen exhaustively via brute-force
experimentation. The addition of just two new components expands this space beyond 10,000,
demonstrating the combinatorial explosion that necessitates an intelligent search strategy. Our
framework was specifically developed to navigate this discrete, noisy, and expensive-to-
evaluate space, providing a practical bridge between theoretical chemistry and real-world
experimental constraints.
b) The search space is also very small – 720, 5400 and 5726. Do we really need AL for such
small spaces? AL is usually carried over large search spaces on the order of thousands, if not
millions, of input samples.
Our response: We agree with the reviewer that these search spaces are not large in a “big data”
context. However, the need for Active Learning (AL) in our work is dictated not by the absolute
size of the search space, but by the prohibitive cost of each experimental evaluation.
In this domain, our total “experimental budget” is severely limited. Each sample requires
months of testing and occupies a channel on our specialized equipment. Therefore, our primary
objective is to achieve maximum sample efficiency—to locate the optimal formulation in the
fewest possible experimental steps.
high query cost, where it intelligently selects the next most informative experiment to run. By
sequentially learning and updating its model of the landscape, it minimizes the number of costly
evaluations needed to converge on a high-performing candidate. The goal is not to exhaustively
search the space, but to find the optimum with a budget of just a few dozen experiments. Our
two-stage framework further enhances this by allowing the incorporation of new molecules
without restarting the entire process, directly addressing a key limitation in practical research.
Thus, the use of AL is not only justified but essential for making progress in a field
constrained by such severe experimental bottlenecks.
c) A frequentist ML model can well be utilized to find optimal candidates in such small search
spaces.
Our response: While a frequentist ML model could certainly be trained on a completed dataset
to predict performance, it is fundamentally the ill-suited tool for the task of sequential
experimental design, which is the core of our work.
The critical distinction is that a standard frequentist model provides a point estimate (a
single predicted value), but it lacks a measure of its own predictive uncertainty. In a data-
scarce and expensive discovery campaign like the electrolyte discovery problem, this
uncertainty is arguably more important than the prediction itself. It is the uncertainty that
answers the most crucial question: “Which experiment should I run next to find the
optimum most efficiently?”
Our Bayesian active learning framework is designed to answer exactly that question. By
maintaining a full posterior distribution, it quantifies the model’s confidence across the entire
search space. This uncertainty is fed into our Thompson sampling acquisition function, which
naturally balances two critical needs:
• Exploration: Testing in regions where the model is uncertain but the potential could
be high.
• Exploitation: Refining candidates in regions already known to be promising.
A frequentist model, lacking this uncertainty, cannot perform this intelligent exploration
and would resort to a purely exploitative or random search, leading to lower sample efficiency
and a higher risk of converging to a local optimum. Therefore, we chose a Bayesian approach
not just as a preference, but as a necessity for enabling the sample-efficient, guided search
required to solve this problem with high cost of each experiment.
5. In Figure 2e, I believe the comparison between GP-AL and DAL is made using the RBF
covariance kernel in GPs. While it is true that RBF is suited for smooth and continuous
14
functions, there are also other standard covariance kernels that can be used when there is
roughness in the functions, e.g., Matern, rational quadratic, pairwise, etc. Multiple covariance
kernels can also be combined together to achieve the desired effect. So, their choice of using
DKL over GP in the present study is not well justified. They should compare GPs with
aforementioned covariance kernels to truly establish the superiority of DKL over GPs in such
scenarios.
Our response: We thank the reviewer for the comment and agree that the choice of covariance
kernel critically affects the performance of Gaussian process (GP) models. In Figure 2e, the
baseline GP-AL results were shown with the radial basis function (RBF) kernel, which is a
standard default due to its smoothness assumptions and wide use in Bayesian optimization.
Importantly, our comparison was not restricted to this case. In additional numerical studies, we
explicitly tested GP models with alternative kernels, including the Matern class, as reported in
Supplementary Figs. 3 and 4. While Matern kernels provided some improvement over RBF
in certain synthetic benchmarks, our DAL framework consistently achieved superior
performance across scenarios, indicating that the observed benefits are not an artifact of kernel
choice.
Beyond direct comparisons, the broader motivation for adopting DKL lies in the challenge
of kernel specification in our application domain. Each kernel encodes specific assumptions
about the underlying functional landscape—for example, RBF assumes infinitely differentiable
smoothness, while Matern allows controlled roughness. However, in electrolyte optimization
the true correlation structure among solvents, salts, and additives is highly complex and not
known a priori. Selecting and tuning a fixed kernel, or combining multiple kernels, requires
strong manual assumptions and extensive heuristic effort, which risks mis-specifying the model.
By contrast, DKL provides an adaptive mechanism to learn effective kernel representations
directly from data, enabling the model to flexibly capture the relationships among solvents,
salts, and additives without relying on predetermined smoothness assumptions. This adaptivity
is particularly valuable given the high experimental variability and the complex interactions
among electrolyte formulations in our system.
To improve the justification, the text below has been inserted into the “Deep active
learning approach” Section of the revised manuscript: “On one hand, the deep neural network
can learn structure-property relationships directly from data, automatically forming adaptive
kernel representations and thereby avoiding the need for manually defined covariance kernels
with predefined smoothness assumptions, which enhances the representation ability of models.”
6. Along the same lines, the authors mention that “…the black-box functions with rapid
oscillations, which are characteristic of the objective function in the electrolyte optimization
problem…” But it has not been explicitly shown that the objective function for electrolyte
optimization problem is indeed “rapidly oscillating”.
Our response: By “rapid oscillations,” we refer to the large parameter–performance
discontinuities observed in our experimental data. As shown in Supplementary Fig. 2 (here
cited as Fig. R5 for readability), even when varying only one component (e.g., additive, lithium
salt concentration, salt identity, or solvent), the resulting cycle life shows sharp and non-
monotonic changes, rather than smooth trends. For instance, in Supplementary Figs. 2b, h,
and k, small changes in composition can lead to either significant improvement or drastic
deterioration in lifetime, with no gradual transition. This confirms that the objective function in
electrolyte optimization is indeed highly non-smooth and discontinuous. To improve clarity ,
we have revised the manuscript to explicitly connect the term “rapid oscillations” with the
experimental evidence presented in Supplementary Fig. 2.
As illustrated in Supplementary Fig. 2, the space of electrolyte formulas is discrete in the
dimensions of Li salts, solvents and additives, but somewhat relatively continuous in salt
concentrations (Supplementary Figs. 2d-f), which points to an objective function featuring
both discontinuous transitions and continuous variations. This sharp and non-monotonic
response of cycle life to single-component changes demonstrates the “rapid oscillations” in the
objective function that characterize the electrolyte optimization problem. Therefore, a
numerical function of 𝑓 =(1−|𝑥|)sin(20(1−|𝑥|)6) was set up to simulate the process to
verify the efficacy of the DAL approach based on the surrogate model of DKL (Fig. 2e and
detailed in Methods).
7. The authors also make claims about DAL framework being able to balance between exploration and exploitation. This
can be explicitly shown on a reduced latent space representation of electrolytes from the trained DKL model by showing
suggestions from different batches. If the model is indeed exploiting, then the suggestions from later batches should
converge to a particular region of the chemical space. The authors can also show distribution of uncertainties for
suggestions from different batches and if the model is progressing towards exploitation, then the distribution of uncertainties
should shift towards lower values.
Our response: Thank you for your comment. In fact, the dynamics of balancing exploration and
exploitation during the DAL optimization are already reflected in Supplementary Fig. 5 (here
cited as Fig. R6 for readability). Specifically:
First, iteration improvement (Fig. R6a and b): The cycle life of the tested electrolytes
shows consistent enhancement across iterations, with progressively diminishing gains (Fig.
S6b). This trend demonstrates that the model initially explores a broader parameter space but
gradually shifts towards exploitation by converging to high-performing regions.
Second, exploration-exploitation balance (Fig. R6c): The overlap of the suggested
candidates between the third and fourth iterations (orange points in the red box) highlights
exploitation, as the model repeatedly focuses on promising regions. Meanwhile, the blue points
with relatively high uncertainty illustrate the continuing element of exploration, maintaining
diversity in the search.
Together, these results confirm that the DAL framework naturally achieves a balance
between exploration and exploitation, consistent with the reviewer’s expectation.
8. How are the molecular components represented? I do not see any discussion in the Methods section. Do they represent molecules using Morgan fingerprints or RDKit features or graph neural networks (GNN) or some sort of one-hot encoding? If one-hot encoding is used to represent molecular components in the electrolytes, then their model cannot really be inferred on molecular components unseen by the DKL model. If that’s the case, then the claim of “optimization over discrete electrolyte space” again does not really hold true.
Our response: We thank the reviewer for raising this point. Representation of molecular
components is indeed central to our framework. We acknowledge that molecular fingerprints
(e.g., Morgan), RDKit features, and graph neural networks (GNNs) are powerful tools for
cheminformatics, as they encode detailed structural and physicochemical information. However,
these approaches are fundamentally designed for large-scale datasets. They rely on thousands
or even millions of labeled molecules to learn stable representations and to generalize robustly
to unseen structures. In contrast, electrolyte discovery operates under radically different
conditions: each data point requires weeks to months of electrochemical testing, experimental
reproducibility is limited, and datasets are inevitably small, sparse, and noisy. These constraints
make the aforementioned complex representations impractical, leading to inaccurate models
and a high risk of overfitting. . Our approach therefore emphasizes a representation strategy
that is both experimentally feasible and aligned with the discrete, high-cost nature of electrolyte
optimization. Specifically:
(1) Representation strategy. In practice, we do not rely on simple one-hot encoding, which
would restrict the model to a closed set of molecules and prevent generalization. Instead, each
electrolyte formulation is represented by relational features that capture pairwise, triplet, and
higher-order interactions among salts, solvents, additives, and concentrations. These features
are quantified using the average degree of interaction (ADI), defined as the mean cycle life
across all tested formulations containing a given component combination. For example, the
ADI between DOL and EC reflects the average cycle life measured across all electrolytes that
include both solvents. This representation embeds experimentally derived interaction
knowledge into the feature space and can be incrementally refined as additional data or new
components are incorporated. Such adaptability is integral to our two-stage framework, in
which knowledge obtained from smaller, well-characterized spaces is systematically
transferred to larger or newly expanded spaces, thereby ensuring both scalability and continuity
of optimization under realistic experimental conditions.
(2) Why not molecular fingerprints or GNNs. These molecular representations are
indeed powerful tools in cheminformatics, as they encode detailed structural and
physicochemical information and can, in principle, generalize to unseen molecules. However,
their effectiveness relies on access to large, diverse, and well-labeled datasets. In electrolyte
discovery, each new data point requires costly preparation and long-term cycling tests (often
extending over weeks or months) making the collection of datasets at the scale required for
graph- or fingerprint-based approaches impractical. Our study instead targets discrete
electrolyte formulations, where the dominant challenge is to extract meaningful knowledge
from scarce but high-value data. Relational features derived directly from experimental
outcomes provide a more practical and chemically aligned representation, as they capture
transferable interaction knowledge that can be reused when the search space expands. This
allows subsequent optimization to fully leverage prior insights rather than restarting from
scratch, thereby improving efficiency under realistic experimental constraints.
(3) Handling unseen components. We agree with the reviewer that predicting performance
for entirely new molecules is inherently challenging. Our framework is not intended for zero-
data prediction of unseen components, but rather supports few-shot transfer. When a new
solvent, salt, or additive is introduced, a limited number of targeted experiments are conducted
to estimate its pairwise ADI values with existing components. Once these priors are established,
the model can incorporate the new component into the optimization process while leveraging
the interaction knowledge already captured from the existing component library. Importantly,
this adaptive mechanism allows the framework to expand iteratively over time,
incorporating new molecules and enlarging the search space without the need for
complete retraining.

Our response: We thank the reviewer for this important comment. The reviewer is correct that
the Average Degree of Interaction (ADI) values are calculated post-training. ADI is not intended
to be a predictive feature learned by the model itself, but rather a post-hoc abstraction of the
knowledge captured by the trained DKL surrogate. It serves to distill the complex, non-linear
component interactions into an interpretable and transferable format.
The core of the reviewer’s concern is how to handle entirely new molecules. Our
framework is designed for efficient few-shot optimization, not for zero-shot prediction, which
remains a largely unsolved problem in experimental chemistry. When introducing a novel
component, we initialize its interaction values with the mean ADI of existing components. This
approach provides an informed, neutral prior—a more principled starting point than a random
guess—from which the active learning loop can begin.
The key is that this initial prior is not the final word; it is the starting point for exploration.
The framework is designed to leverage this prior to select the most informative initial
experiments involving the new molecule, allowing it to learn that molecule’s specific
interaction profile with maximum efficiency. This stands in sharp contrast to conventional
methods, which would require restarting the optimization from scratch and discarding all
previously acquired knowledge.
The practical power of this strategy is demonstrated in our results. As shown in Fig. 5b,
our framework successfully identified a high-performing formulation containing new
molecular components within a single iteration of active learning. This result validates that the
TSC-based knowledge transfer, even when initiated with a simple prior, dramatically
accelerates discovery in expanded chemical spaces.

Our response: We thank the reviewer for this valuable comment. The use of deep kernel learning
(DKL) and Thompson sampling (TS) in our framework is a methodological necessity dictated
by the unique characteristics of electrolyte discovery in this work. Conventional BO methods—
based on smooth surrogate functions and sequential sampling—are often effective for
continuous, well-behaved optimization landscapes. However, electrolyte design exhibits
fundamentally different characteristics. As shown in Supplementary Fig. 2, even a small
variation in formulation (e.g., changing an additive, lithium salt concentration, or solvent) can
lead to sharp, non-monotonic changes in cycle life, resulting in a highly discontinuous and
multimodal objective surface. These characteristics violate the smoothness assumptions
inherent to standard Gaussian Process (GP) models.
Moreover, our experimental platform that is a 32-channel battery cycler allows
simultaneous testing of multiple electrolyte formulations, making large-batch parallel
exploration essential to accelerate the optimization process optimization under costly and time-
intensive evaluations. Our adoption of DKL and TS is thus driven by both the need for an
adaptive mechanism to learn effective kernel representations and efficient large-batch parallel
exploration, as elaborated below.
as the radial basis function (RBF), which encodes infinitely differentiable smoothness. This
assumption becomes restrictive when modeling the discrete and compositionally nonlinear
landscape of electrolyte formulations. DKL mitigates this limitation by introducing a learnable
kernel structure:

DKL base
where 𝑘 (𝒙,𝒙′) denotes the base kernel function, 𝜽 is the hyperparameter of the base
base
kernel, and 𝑔 is the nonlinear mapping learned by the deep neural network, which is
parameterized by the weights 𝝎.
By maximizing the marginal likelihood of DKL, we learn all deep kernel hyperparameters,
including the parameter 𝝎 of the deep neural network and the parameter 𝜽 of the base kernel.
The kernel function in (1) achieves adaptive learning from the data by leveraging the flexible
representational capabilities of deep neural networks while maintaining the robust uncertainty
quantification inherent to Gaussian processes. This stands in contrast to standard GP methods
that use traditional kernels, which are constrained by predefined similarity metrics. We
demonstrate the superior effectiveness of our proposed DKL approach in Fig. 2D of the revised
manuscript, where it successfully captures the complex relationships in electrolyte optimization
that elude conventional kernels.
Thompson sampling (TS). Efficient parallel exploration is a critical requirement imposed
by our experimental workflow. Each experimental round is costly and time-consuming, yet our
platform enables simultaneous testing of multiple electrolyte formulations. To fully leverage
this capability and accelerate the optimization process, we need to select a diverse and
promising batch of candidates at each iteration rather than a single point.
Thompson Sampling is well-suited for this batch scenario. To generate a batch of 𝑘
candidates (in our case, 𝑘=32), we can simply draw 𝑘 independent function samples from the
posterior of the Gaussian Process surrogate model. The location of the maximum of each
sample is then chosen as a candidate for the batch. This procedure is computationally efficient
and naturally promotes exploration and diversity within the batch [R1], as each sample
represents a different plausible hypothesis of the true objective function. In contrast, extending
the commonly used acquisition functions in standard BO like Expected Improvement (EI) to
the batch setting is more complex. A naive approach of simply selecting the top 𝑘 points with
the highest EI values would result in a highly redundant batch, with points clustered around a
single peak in the acquisition function. More sophisticated methods like q-Expected
Improvement (q-EI) are required to properly account for the joint improvement over a batch,
but they come at a much higher computational cost and implementation complexity [R2]. Given
our experimental constraint of performing 32 parallel evaluations, TS offers an elegant, scalable,
and effective acquisition strategy for maximizing the efficiency of our discovery workflow.

REVIEWER COMMENTS
Reviewer #1 (Remarks to the Author):
The manuscript has been revised pretty well according to the 1st round review. All my concerns
have been well addressed and I believe this work can cause wide interests and broad impact.
Our response: We thank the reviewer for the positive assessment and are grateful for the helpful

Reviewer #2 (Remarks to the Author):
The authors have provided a detailed response to my comments in the first round of revision and
many of my comments have been satisfactorily addressed, including the release of codes and
datasets. However, some critical comments remain unaddressed. See below:
1. Comment #2 in the first round on predicting aleatoric uncertainties has not been taken care of but
can be addressed. I recommend the authors to follow this reference for guidance: Zhong et al., Nat.
Commun. 16, 4522 (2025). Predicting aleatoric uncertainties is critical for quantifying
reproducibility in the experimental measurements.
Our response: We thank the reviewer for emphasizing the importance of explicitly modeling
aleatoric uncertainty and for pointing us to the recent work by Zhong et al. (Nat. Commun. 16, 4522,
2025). Disentangling aleatoric and epistemic uncertainties is valuable for assessing experimental
reproducibility and robustness. From an algorithmic perspective, Zhong et al. decompose predictive
uncertainty by sampling from the posterior distribution of network weights, defining the aleatoric
component as the expected predictive entropy under fixed model parameters and the epistemic
component as the residual uncertainty induced by variability across weight samples. In contrast, our
framework employs a Gaussian process with deep kernel learning under a homoscedastic noise
assumption, in which observation noise is treated as input-independent. As a result, while the model
provides well-calibrated predictive uncertainty that primarily reflects epistemic uncertainty arising
from sparse sampling and limited coverage of the compositional design space, it does not explicitly
parameterize input-dependent aleatoric uncertainty. Consequently, a formal decomposition of
predictive uncertainty into aleatoric and epistemic components is not directly supported within the
current modeling formulation.
Importantly, this modeling choice is aligned with the primary objective of our study and is also
consistent with the conclusions reported by Zhong et al. (Nat. Commun. 16, 4522, 2025). In the
small-sample experimental regime considered here, uncertainty estimates are used to guide
exploration-exploitation trade-offs under a limited experimental budget, where epistemic
uncertainty dominates and relative uncertainty rankings are sufficient for identifying informative
1
regions of the search space. Consistent with the findings of Zhong et al., in early-stage active
learning with limited data, uncertainty decomposition provides limited practical benefit due to
unstable epistemic estimates, and acquisition strategies based on overall predictive uncertainty are
more robust and data-efficient, even in the absence of an explicit aleatoric-epistemic separation.
We agree with the reviewer that extending the present framework to explicitly model input-
dependent aleatoric uncertainty represents an important direction for future work. While the current
DKL-GP formulation adopts a homoscedastic noise assumption, future work will consider
heteroscedastic Gaussian process models to explicitly capture input-dependent experimental noise,
thereby improving uncertainty decomposition and reproducibility-oriented analyses. We have now
explicitly acknowledged this limitation and the corresponding future research direction in the
Discussion section of the revised manuscript.
2. Comparison of t-SNE plots of all electrolytes (suggested ones should be clearly highlighted) from

for guidance: Khalak et al., J. Chem. Theory Comput. 18, 6259-6270 (2022) (Figure 5).
Our response: We thank the reviewer for this suggestion. Low-dimensional visualizations are
powerful for illustrating how an algorithm explores a complex design space. In Khalak et al. (J.
Chem. Theory Comput. 18, 6259-6270 (2022)), t-SNE is applied to a molecular encoding space,
where each molecule is represented by a high-dimensional descriptor vector. In that context, the
high dimensionality arises primarily from the choice of molecular descriptors and encoding scheme,
and t-SNE is well suited to reveal latent structure in this continuous, descriptor-based chemical
space.
In our work, however, the underlying design problem is fundamentally different. We do not
optimize over individual molecular structures, but over electrolyte formulations, which are defined
by a finite set of discrete components (salt, solvent, additive) and their concentrations. Here, the
increase in dimensionality is driven by the combinatorial diversity of component types and mixing
ratios, rather than by a continuous, high-dimensional molecular descriptor space. Encoding each
formulation into a high-dimensional vector (e.g., via one-hot representations of component
identities) and then applying t-SNE would mainly reflect the arbitrary categorical encoding of the
formulation space, rather than a physically meaningful notion of molecular similarity. As a result,
the apparent “clusters” in such a t-SNE map would largely be determined by how the categories are
encoded, and would not necessarily provide additional mechanistic insight into the electrolyte
behavior.
For this reason, instead of using a t-SNE embedding of a formulation encoding, we adopted a

formulations are designed and interpreted. In the revised manuscript, we explicitly analyze how

discarded, and it directly reflects the way experimentalists reason about multi-component

electrolytes.

3. The authors’ reasons for not using any chemical representation in the present framework is not
justified (point #8 in the first round). If data-scarcity was the issue then one can use a pretrained
model to generate molecular features for solvents, salts, and additives and feed to the surrogate
model. The current approach may not lead to any new molecular design of electrolytes in a zero-
shot manner, which stands in contrast to their claims of “optimization over discrete electrolyte
space”.
Our response: We thank the reviewer for this point and for highlighting the possibility of using
pretrained molecular representations. The molecular foundation models are becoming central to de
novo molecular design, and pretrained encoders can provide rich molecular features for solvents,
salts, and additives.
Our goal in this work, however, is more modest and differs in scope from de novo, zero-shot
molecular design. We focus on data-efficient optimization of electrolyte formulations for long-
term cycle life within a fixed, experimentally accessible library of salts, solvents, and additives,
under a specific cycling protocol. Each labeled data point corresponds to a full-cell life test that
typically requires months to complete and is strongly influenced by electrodes, cell geometry,
formation procedures, and test conditions. Consequently, the number of reliably labeled
formulations in our study is orders of magnitude smaller than the 104–106 molecules or mixtures
typically used to train or fine-tune current chemical foundation models, which are often built on
MD-derived structural descriptors, transport properties, or equilibrium thermodynamic quantities.
In principle, one could take an existing pretrained molecular encoder and use it to generate
fixed embeddings for the solvents, salts, and additives in our library, and then feed these embeddings
into the DKL surrogate model. In our setting, however, the main challenge is not only data scarcity,
but also task and domain misalignment between available pretrained models and our target
property. Existing electrolyte-related foundation models are generally pretrained on simulated or
literature-derived data that emphasize equilibrium or short-timescale properties (e.g., solvation
structure, ionic conductivity, viscosity, density). By contrast, the cycle life of a full cell over
hundreds of cycles is governed by long-timescale interfacial degradation, parasitic reactions, gas
evolution, and coupled electrode-electrolyte failure mechanisms, which are only indirectly reflected
in those pretraining tasks. In a small-data regime such as ours, adding high-dimensional molecular
embeddings that are not well aligned with the target property can in fact make the surrogate harder
to train and less stable, without guaranteeing a corresponding gain in predictive power.
Importantly, our current framework does not omit chemical information; rather, it adopts a
formulation-centric chemical representation that is tightly coupled to the experimental objective.
Instead of representing individual molecules in a continuous descriptor space, we encode
experimentally derived interaction descriptors such as the ADI for pairs and higher-order
combinations of components. These features summarize, in a low-dimensional and task-specific
way, how particular combinations of salts, solvents, and additives affect the observed cycle life
across all available formulations. As new experiments are performed, these interaction descriptors
are updated, providing an end-to-end, experiment-driven representation that directly reflects the
“composition-structure-performance” relationship relevant to long-term cycling stability.
This design has two practical consequences. First, it enables combinatorial optimization over
a large discrete formulation space spanned by a fixed library of experimentally accessible
components, which is the actual focus of this work. Second, it naturally supports few-shot expansion
of the space: when a new component is introduced, only a small number of targeted experiments are
needed to estimate its interaction descriptors with existing components, after which it can be
seamlessly integrated into the optimization loop without retraining a separate molecular encoder.
To avoid overstating our current capabilities, we have revised the wording of our claims in the
Abstract and Discussion. Specifically, we replace “optimization over discrete electrolyte space”
with “optimization of formulations within a fixed discrete component library”. We also add a short
paragraph in the Discussion outlining how pretrained molecular representation models could be
integrated into our framework in future work, once sufficiently large and task-aligned pretraining
datasets for long-term cycling performance become available.

to points #8 and #9). We explicitly state that the current framework optimizes over
combinatorial electrolyte formulations built from a fixed, experimentally accessible

solvents, salts, or additives still require targeted experiments before they can be

2. Highlight the limitations of our formulation-centric representation and the TSC/ADI
scheme (related to points #8 and #9). We emphasize that chemical information is encoded
via interaction statistics (e.g., ADIs) rather than detailed molecule-level embeddings, and
that TSC and ADI are post-hoc abstractions. This design is pragmatic for small, noisy

3. Explicitly acknowledge limitations in uncertainty modeling (related to point #2). We
clarify that the current framework models uncertainty under a homoscedastic noise
assumption, and therefore does not explicitly disentangle or quantify input-dependent
aleatoric uncertainty. While this choice is appropriate for small-sample active learning
where epistemic uncertainty dominates, extending the framework to heteroscedastic
uncertainty modeling is considered as an important direction for future work and is now
explicitly discussed.

explicitly quantified, which constrains the assessment of experimental variability and

I appreciate the response of the authors to my comments. I think the questions are overall very well
presented. However, the answer to my Comment #4 is vague. I cannot find the details about the
improvements completed by the author. The improvements to enhanced the significant of this work
to the audience is highly essential. I hope this point can be addressed further.
Our response: We thank the reviewer for the follow-up comment, and we apologize that our previous
response did not clearly describe the corresponding revisions. In the revised manuscript, we have
implemented several concrete changes to make the interdisciplinary significance of this work more
explicit for both battery and machine-learning audiences:
1. Abstract (last two sentences). We have rewritten the final two sentences of the Abstract
to clearly state what the framework offers to each community. This change is intended to
explicitly communicate the relevance of our framework to both readerships at the very
beginning of the paper. The Abstract now ends with: “This work provides an experiment-
driven, sample-efficient route to explore complex electrolyte formulation spaces and
quantify inter-component correlations, as well as a realistic, high-cost, small-data
benchmark for probabilistic surrogate modeling and sequential decision-making in discrete
chemical spaces. Together, these advances establish an AI-assisted discovery framework
for rapid exploration, knowledge learning and transfer in complex materials spaces, without
relying on detailed mechanistic models or empirical design rules.”
2. Introduction (new “bridge” sentence). At the end of the Introduction, we have added an
explicit bridging sentence that summarizes what each community can take away from the
DAL–TSC workflow:
“From the perspective of battery research, this framework organizes costly cycling
experiments into a structured, sample-efficient exploration of electrolyte formulations;
from the perspective of machine learning, it provides a realistic, high-cost and small-data
testbed for probabilistic surrogate modeling and sequential decision-making in discrete
chemical spaces.”
